There is a simple reason why some people sound more educated in a second language than others, and it has very little to do with vocabulary. It is the length of the thought. A speaker who only has and, but and because has to stop every six or seven words and start again, so even a clever idea arrives in small pieces. A speaker who also has although, whereas and despite can hold two opposing ideas in the same sentence, and that is exactly what an educated argument sounds like. Yes, this is true, and at the same time, this other thing is also true. You do not need difficult words to do it. You need about five small connectors, and the confidence to keep the sentence going until the second half arrives.

Our city closed the main street to cars two years ago, and I was against it. I drove to work every day, and I was sure the shops would lose customers. Although I still drive, I have to admit that I was mostly wrong. The shops did not close. In fact, despite the complaints in the first few months, most of them now have more people walking past than before. However, it has not been good for everybody. Small businesses that depend on deliveries say their costs have gone up, whereas the cafes and restaurants are doing better than ever. So when people ask me now whether it was a good idea, I give the answer I like least. It depends on who you ask.
